test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 14 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: 8 men and 3 women can complete a piece of work in 15 days, and 14 men and 19 women can complete the same work in 5 days. The work of how many women is equivalent to that of one man?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Equating total work using M₁ × D₁ = M₂ × D₂:

⇒ (8M + 3W) × 15 = (14M + 19W) × 5

⇒ 3 × (8M + 3W) = 1 × (14M + 19W)

⇒ 24M + 9W = 14M + 19W

⇒ 10M = 10W ⇒ 1M = 1W

**∴ The correct answer is 1 woman.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Group 1: 8 Men and 3 Women can do the work in 15 days.

Group 2: 14 Men and 19 Women can do the work in 5 days.

**Formula Used:**

Total Work = LCM of Days

Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Days

**Calculations:**

 
 

 **Person**
 **Days**
 **Total Work**
 **Efficiency**
 
 

 8 Men + 3 Women
 15
 15
 15 ÷ 15 = 1
 
 

 14 Men + 19 Women
 5
 15 ÷ 5 = 3
 
 

⇒ Efficiency of (8 Men + 3 Women) = 1 unit/day

⇒ Efficiency of (14 Men + 19 Women) = 3 units/day

⇒ Multiplying the first equation by 3 to equate the efficiencies:

⇒ 3 × (8 Men + 3 Women) = 14 Men + 19 Women

⇒ 24 Men + 9 Women = 14 Men + 19 Women

⇒ 24 Men − 14 Men = 19 Women − 9 Women

⇒ 10 Men = 10 Women

⇒ 1 Man = 1 Woman

**∴ The correct answer is 1 woman.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Chain Rule (MDH Concept)

If two different groups complete the same amount of work, their total work can be equated directly as (M₁ × D₁) = (M₂ × D₂).

Total Work & Efficiency

Efficiency is inversely proportional to the number of days taken. Hence, the ratio of efficiencies for two groups doing the same work is the reciprocal of the ratio of their days taken.

Equating Different Entities

In men-women problems, always balance the work equations to find a straightforward ratio between the daily efficiencies of one man and one woman.
